power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Below, we describe some best coding practices and give the results of automatic evaluation of these practices in the code files below. This check may miss things or produce false positives if your scripts are less typical.
#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. The following absolute file paths were found in 2 code files. However, these may be false positives in code like `paste0(dir, '/file.csv')`.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports
Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.
#### Packages / Dependencies
The code files load 3 distinct packages/libraries: data.table, httr, jsonlite. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.

We encountered parsing issues when trying to read in R-type code files. The following errors were found in 2 code files:

text.text: Rare diseases represent a major public health challenge because they are often associated with severe phenotypes, yet many causal variants remain undiscovered.
Founder populations provide a unique opportunity to identify disease-causing variants through the local enrichment of rare alleles.

Using whole-genome sequencing data from individuals in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean population, enriched variants were identified and their founder status was assessed through identity-by-descent sharing.
Variant impact was evaluated using functional prediction tools without relying on prior clinical classification.
A total of 131 founder variants of interest were identified, most of which would likely have been overlooked by conventional approaches based on existing clinical annotations.
We developed a web-based platform that facilitates clinician access to the latest interpretation of their genetic variants of interest.
These findings demonstrate that potentially pathogenic variants can remain undetected even in extensively studied founder populations.

More broadly, they highlight the value of population structure-based approaches for uncovering rare disease variants and improving the characterization of genetic disease risk across human populations.
Rare diseases tend to have more severe clinical consequences than common conditions [1].
text.formatted: Rare diseases tend to have more severe clinical consequences than common conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Although each disorder affects only a small number of individuals, their combined prevalence is substantial, making rare diseases a significant public-health concern and a considerable burden for patients and families [2, 3].
text.formatted: Although each disorder affects only a small number of individuals, their combined prevalence is substantial, making rare diseases a significant public-health concern and a considerable burden for patients and families <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: The major challenge of studying rare disease-causing variants lies in their low frequency in the broad population, which makes them difficult to detect and characterize.

Founder populations have deeply contributed to overcome this obstacle: their demographic history increases the frequency of certain rare variants [4] https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?qVwULh creating a context in which both these variants and their associated phenotypes become observable [5] [6] [7] [8].
text.formatted: Founder populations have deeply contributed to overcome this obstacle: their demographic history increases the frequency of certain rare variants <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?qVwULh">,</ref> creating a context in which both these variants and their associated phenotypes become observable <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Most rare disease studies rely on clinically well-defined variants catalogued in databases such as ClinVar, for which the associated phenotypes are already established [9].
text.formatted: Most rare disease studies rely on clinically well-defined variants catalogued in databases such as ClinVar, for which the associated phenotypes are already established <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: However, focusing primarily on such variants limits the identification of novel pathogenic variants, especially those lacking clinical evidence for classification and therefore categorized as variants of uncertain significance (VUS).
Consequently, variants contributing to atypical or unrecognized phenotypes may remain overlooked.
This challenge is reflected in clinical practice, where approximately 22.5% of exome and genome sequencing results remain inconclusive because of VUS [10].
text.formatted: This challenge is reflected in clinical practice, where approximately 22.5% of exome and genome sequencing results remain inconclusive because of VUS <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: These limitations highlight the need for population contexts where rare pathogenic variants can be detected independently of prior clinical classification.
Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean (SLSJ) region in Quebec, Canada, represents one of the most thoroughly studied founder populations [11, 12].
text.formatted: Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean (SLSJ) region in Quebec, Canada, represents one of the most thoroughly studied founder populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: Despite decades of genetic research and the identification of numerous disease-associated founder variantshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?BQeTd8 the clinically relevant variation present in this population remains incompletely characterized [13] and recent studies continue to uncover enriched pathogenic founder variants in the SLSJ population [13] [14] [15] [16] , suggesting that additional clinically relevant variation may remain undetected.
text.formatted: Despite decades of genetic research and the identification of numerous disease-associated founder variants, the clinically relevant variation present in this population remains incompletely characterized <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> and recent studies continue to uncover enriched pathogenic founder variants in the SLSJ population <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?BQeTd8">,</ref> suggesting that additional clinically relevant variation may remain undetected.

text.text: This study aims to identify novel founder variants in SLSJ by leveraging population structure rather than clinical classification, and to evaluate their potential functional impact and clinical relevance.
In founder populations, patterns of IBD sharing can reveal variants introduced by a common ancestor, as these variants typically reside on shared haplotypes.
Combined with evidence of population enrichment, these signatures provide a powerful means of detecting rare variants independently of existing clinical annotations or classification.

To support the translation of these findings into clinical practice, this project will also develop a web-based resource enabling clinicians to rapidly access the population and genetic context of encountered variants, thereby improving the prioritization and interpretation of variants with potential clinical significance.
Detailed methods can be found in Supplementary material.

Potential founder variants in the SLSJ were identified in whole-genome sequences (WGS) from 817 individuals from the SLSJ and 1,696 from elsewhere in Quebec according to multiple selection criteria (See methods).

Based solely on their increased frequency in individuals from the SLSJ region compared with other regions of Quebec (≥10%), more than 11 million variants were initially identified as potential founder variants (Fig. 1), highlighting the need for additional criteria.
text.formatted: Based solely on their increased frequency in individuals from the SLSJ region compared with other regions of Quebec (≥10%), more than 11 million variants were initially identified as potential founder variants (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), highlighting the need for additional criteria.

text.text: Among these, only 0,4% were both located within the Consensus Coding Sequence (CCDS) and carried by enough individuals for downstream analyses.
Following all founder variant criteria, 14,621 variants remained, underscoring the need for additional prioritization criteria.
Of these, 5,96% were predicted to be likely pathogenic by AlphaMissense, while 0,896% had additionally a high pLI score.

To further prioritize variants with a higher likelihood of functional impact, we focused on variants located in genes intolerant to loss-of-function mutations (pLI >0.9), yielding a final set of 131 candidate variants (Fig. 2; Supplementary Table 1).
text.formatted: To further prioritize variants with a higher likelihood of functional impact, we focused on variants located in genes intolerant to loss-of-function mutations (pLI >0.9), yielding a final set of 131 candidate variants (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The approach used in this study enabled the identification of numerous previously undocumented variants of potential interest in SLSJ.

These findings demonstrate that leveraging population structure rather than clinical classification uncovers variants that would otherwise remain undetected due to mild phenotypes or low frequency in the broad population, which limits their inclusion in clinical databases [9, 18].
text.formatted: These findings demonstrate that leveraging population structure rather than clinical classification uncovers variants that would otherwise remain undetected due to mild phenotypes or low frequency in the broad population, which limits their inclusion in clinical databases <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18]</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, the approach uncovered 131 founder variants with potential proteinmodifying effects.
Remarkably, despite their higher frequency in SLSJ, these variants had remained undetected even in this thoroughly studied founder population [11, 12].
text.formatted: Remarkably, despite their higher frequency in SLSJ, these variants had remained undetected even in this thoroughly studied founder population <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: This represents a substantial number when compared to the 72 previously known disease-associated rare variants [6https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?zgjhni 11, 12, 17] , or even the 42 reported in a recent population-based study [13].
text.formatted: This represents a substantial number when compared to the 72 previously known disease-associated rare variants <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?zgjhni">,</ref> or even the 42 reported in a recent population-based study <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: As these newly identified founder variants have frequencies similar to those of disease-associated variants, it is plausible that the burden of rare diseases in SLSJ may be greater than previously recognized [6, [11] [12] [13] 17].
text.formatted: As these newly identified founder variants have frequencies similar to those of disease-associated variants, it is plausible that the burden of rare diseases in SLSJ may be greater than previously recognized <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>.

text.text: However, many of these variants would likely remain unnoticed under traditional rare variant identification approaches.
Rare variant studies typically prioritize variants classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic in ClinVar [5, 13].
text.formatted: Rare variant studies typically prioritize variants classified as pathogenic or likely pathogenic in ClinVar <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: Under such an approach, the variants identified here would have been overlooked despite their founder status, as most are absent from the database or classified as VUS.

Although some are currently classified as benign or likely benign in ClinVar, their predicted impact on the protein remains noteworthy and justifies keeping them under consideration, particularly given that variant classifications may be revised as new evidence emerges [19].
text.formatted: Although some are currently classified as benign or likely benign in ClinVar, their predicted impact on the protein remains noteworthy and justifies keeping them under consideration, particularly given that variant classifications may be revised as new evidence emerges <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: To facilitate variant's interpretation as most are absent from ClinVar, a web-based resource was developed as part of this project, providing clinicians with direct access to population-based metrics and the likelihood of the variant to be pathogenic.
This resource represents an important step toward addressing the challenge posed by VUS, which continues to be a major obstacle in clinical practice.
By facilitating the identification of recurrent variants across clinical reports, the resource may support variant interpretation and help prioritize candidate variants for future functional studies.
Some limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, this approach is well suited for detecting recessive founder variants, but has limited ability to identify dominant variants.
This limitation is illustrated by myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), a dominantly inherited genetic disorder enriched in SLSJ, yet present in only 0,16% of participants in CaG [20].
text.formatted: This limitation is illustrated by myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), a dominantly inherited genetic disorder enriched in SLSJ, yet present in only 0,16% of participants in CaG <ref type="bibr">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Given the minimum carrier threshold applied in this study, it is therefore plausible that unidentified dominant disease-causing variants would occur at frequencies too low to be retained for analysis.

Second, the lack of functional validation limits the interpretation and classification of the identified variants, as no phenotypic evidence is available to support a causal relationship between a variant and disease.
Despite these limitations, the present study provides a more comprehensive portrait of the genetic variation present in the SLSJ population.

By reporting and documenting numerous previously unreported rare founder variants in a web-based resource, this study offers a valuable tool for future research aimed at assessing their clinical significance and potential association with rare diseases.
Some of the currently unexplained phenotypes observed in the clinics may be attributable to these variants, highlighting the importance of documenting them.
More broadly, these findings demonstrate that substantial genetic variation can remain unreported even in a thoroughly studied founder population such as SLSJ.
This suggests that similar hidden variants may exist in other founder populations for which the presented approach could be applied.
